contract: C11, the input stage: docs/contracts/C11.md, the part "The input stage (board ab-t30.6)", from the input design (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-10-vanilla-playwright-human-input-design.md, sections 4 to 8, 12.1 point 6 and 13.1) and the operator's answers to Q1 to Q4 (option a each, board item ab-0z5). The stage is not built yet (board tasks ab-t30.9 to ab-t30.12, behind a build switch): these vectors are the contract that the build follows. For each row of the design's table of every input path (section 5.1) the vectors give the client calls in, the events out (the method, the type and the key fields; each time as a range) and the order of the answers, with a seed and a fake clock. The stage's tests (a fake bridge, a fake clock) and test/contracts-c11.test.ts read them.

format.vector: id; row (the first cell of a row of the input design's table, section 5.1, exactly) or rule (the lead of a bullet of C11's part on the input stage); note; platform (linux or mac); seed (the generator's seed); clock (the fake clock's ms at the start); page (the fake page's facts: viewport, last (the page's last point or null), nodes (by the objectId of the node's handle: tag, type, role, box in its frame's own CSS px, the length of its text, focused, frame), focused, frames, scrollers); chrome (optional: how the fake Chrome answers, below); in; out; answers.
format.in: The client calls, in the order in which the client sends them: id; at (ms on the fake clock), or after (the id of the call whose answer makes the client send this one, as Playwright's await does), or afterEvent (an event of Chrome that the client gets); waitMs (the client's own wait after that); session (child: the session of a cross-origin frame; else the tab's own session); method; params (as the client sends them). A utility call carries Playwright 1.65.0's function text.
format.out: What the stage sends to Chrome, in the order in which it sends it: method; type; for (the id of the client call whose plan holds the event); from (start, in:<id> (the arrival of a call) or out:<k> (the last event of an earlier item)) and at ([lo, hi] ms after it); rule (the first value that bounds at, when one does); fields (the key fields: a number is exact, [lo, hi] is a range; a point is in the top page's CSS px). pass: the client's call as it sent it, with the stage's timestamp for an input call. path: the moves of a path from a point to a point (part outside or inside of a box, for a hover; until dragIntercepted and rest, for a drag), one each gapMs, count [lo, hi] moves, durMs [lo, hi] from its first move to its last. line: the samples of a short move. notches: that many wheel events, gapMs [lo, hi] apart. typing: the text as typed keys (a keyDown and a keyUp for each character, a Shift rawKeyDown and keyUp around each character of shift), each hold in holdMs.
format.answers: The answers of the client calls, in the order in which the stage gives them: id; after (out:<k>: the item whose events the answer follows, and Chrome's answer to them; none: an answer of the stage with no event, with its result); mayBeEarly and before (a keyUp's early answer, which comes before out:<k> when the plan says that the next key can overlap); waits (the id of a call whose answer comes first: a dialog's answer); error (chrome: Chrome's error; the same: the error of the plan's refused event); from and at (a later time, with its rule).
format.chrome: results (by in id: Chrome's result for a passed call); events (Chrome's events, at the time of an out item; toClient false: an event of the stage's own interception, which no client gets); dialog (opensAt and closesAt: while the dialog is open, Chrome answers no input event, and after it closes it answers them in order); errors (by out item: Chrome's error for that event). Every other call gets {} at once.
format.times: Each range holds for every seed: its bounds come from C11's constants and first values (constants, firstValues). A range with no rule is an order with a wide bound (a person's time from one key press to the next has no bound in C11).

vectors.row: `mouse.move(x, y)` with a held button over an HTML5 draggable (`mouse.down()` first)
vectors.note: mouse.move(100, 440), mouse.down(), mouse.move(700, 450), mouse.up() over a draggable card. Playwright's drag manager turns Input.setInterceptDrags on before the move with the button down. The stage waits 100 to 300 ms after the press, sends a short path with the button down until Chrome reports Input.dragIntercepted (here at out:3), then its own dragEnter and dragOver events along the rest of the path. Playwright's own dragEnter at the target goes as a dragOver; its drop goes after a pause. (Playwright's utility calls that set up and read its drag listeners pass unchanged, and the vector leaves them out.)
mouse.down() and mouse.up() at the page's last point: no path, so no pause; the release at the later of its arrival and a person's hold.
mouse.click(640, 360) from 900,700: no checks, no spread (a mouse click is no condition 1).
mouse.wheel(0, 600): five notches of 120 px (deltaY 120, wheelDeltaY -120 on the page, as a Linux mouse wheel), with a person's gaps, at the page's last point (M6).

Four calls of mouse.wheel(0, 100), each awaited: n = max(0, round((|delta| + r) / 120)), half up, with r the residual in the call's direction. The calls get 1, 1, 1 and 0 notches (r: 0, -20, -40, -60, then +40): 360 px for 400 asked, within one notch. The fourth call gets no event, because earlier notches have already given it. The first notch of a call comes at the later of its arrival and one person's gap after the page's last notch (35 to 90 ms), so the calls of a client that sends them at once give a person's gaps too.
The Mac: until the Mac's wheel model exists, mouse.wheel(0, 600) goes as the client sent it, with the stage's timestamp (with its fraction).

An element 1,680 px below the viewport (its middle at y 2420 in a viewport of 720 px): 17 notches (round(2060 / 120)) at the page's last point, which is a wheel point (no input, no listener; it scrolls the document). After the smooth scroll's 350 ms the stage reads again: the element is in view, and the stage answers {} (M6: 17 notches). In view at once: the click vector.
The Mac: until the Mac's wheel model exists, the stage sends DOM.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded as the client sent it (a script scroll), and counts it.

The wheel point (the input design's section 8.3): the page's last point 640,360 is over a canvas whose page zooms at the wheel (600 x 420 at 350,150), so it is no wheel point, and neither is any point of the 5 x 5 grid over the canvas. The stage tries the points of the grid over the visible part of the scroller (here the viewport), the nearest to the last point first: 640,101 passes. A path goes there, then 17 notches (round(2060 / 120)) one person's gap after the path, then {} after the smooth scroll's 350 ms.

A round that does not move the scroller ends the notches: a listener of the window that is not passive calls preventDefault (the wheel point's rule does not count the listeners of the window and the document, so 640,360 is a wheel point). After the first round of 17 notches and the smooth scroll's 350 ms the document's scroll position is the same, so the stage sends the client's call as it is (a script scroll), and counts it.

An element of a cross-origin frame (400 x 300 at 300,100, no border) that its own document scrolls (2,000 px tall): the frame's session sends the call. The stage reads the box there and maps it to the top page (the frame mapping), reads the top page's scrollers on the frame's owner, and sends the notches on the top page's session at a point over the frame: the page's last point 900,600 is not over the frame, so the nearest point of the 5 x 5 grid over the frame's visible part, 644,358, where the top page's element is the frame's owner. 11 notches (round((1520 - 150) / 120)), one person's gap after the path, bring the element's middle to the frame's middle, then {} after 350 ms.

fill('ab') into a text input 2,100 px below the viewport (C11: a field out of view first gets notches into view, then the click; review-119 N14): the page's last point 640,360 is a wheel point, so 17 notches (round((2415 - 360) / 120)) go there with no DOM.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded; after the smooth scroll's 350 ms the field is in view (its middle at 375), and the focus click goes at its left end (it has text), then Playwright's script and the typed keys.

keyboard.type('Hi') into the focused field: Playwright sends each key's keyDown and keyUp and waits for each answer; its capital H has modifiers 0. The stage sends a Shift press 45 to 95 ms before H (with modifiers 8), the Shift release 15 to 60 ms after H's release, and i only after both. The answer of each keyUp can come early (before the release goes) when the plan says that the next key can overlap (the stage does not know that i is the last key); the seed decides, so both orders fit the vector.

The stage clicks the field first (an empty textarea: 25% to 75% across, 6 to 12 px from the top), then the utility call passes. The keys of the run follow as in the vector 'type' (left out here).

vectors.note: keyboard.type('ab', { delay: 300 }): Playwright waits 300 ms between each key's press and release. Each release goes at its arrival (the delay is longer than any hold); b's press goes at the later of its arrival and its planned time.

keyboard.press('Control+A'): Playwright presses Control, then A (a rawKeyDown with no text while Control is down), then releases A and Control, each awaited. The stage sends A 40 to 120 ms after Control, holds A, and releases Control 20 to 80 ms after A.

The first key replaces the selection; the @ gets a Shift.

fill('two\nlines') into a focused textarea: no click (it has the focus), and the text has a line feed, so the Input.insertText goes as it is (typing rule 2), after a person's time from one press to the next.
A fill of 114 characters into a focused input: even at the fast end of the spread (100 ms a key) the plan does not fit in STAGE_TYPE_MAX_MS, so the text goes as one Input.insertText (Q2 a).

The gate: a Runtime.evaluate that Playwright sends with the click (not awaited) goes to Chrome only after the release, so it sees the page after the click.

A confirm() in the page's mousedown handler: the dialog opens at the press. Chrome keeps the input events that it got before the dialog opened, and drops those that it gets while the dialog is open (measured by board ab-t30.9: it answers them at once, and the page never gets them). The plan ends: its own events are dropped (the rest of the hold), and the lock is free; the client's release waits for the dialog's close and then goes at once (a hold counts from the press's send). The client's Page.handleJavaScriptDialog goes to Chrome at once, before the tab's gate, and gets its answer first; then Chrome answers the press (kept from before the dialog) and the release (sent after the close).
Chrome refuses the press: the stage stops the plan. The press gets Chrome's error; the release, whose event did not go, gets the same error (no button is down, so no release goes).
